items.title: Turo’s Black Friday Deal: $50 Off Your Holiday Road Trip
items.summary:
Turo’s a fun way to rent cars you wouldn’t find at an airport counter. Plus, you get to pick a specific vehicle, rather than “whatever, or similar” that big rental brands give you. Turo’s peer-to-peer car rental setup is now running a holiday promo, and first-time American renters can use code TURO50TT to get $50 off a reservation of $250 or more.

The fine print: the code works from November 26 through December 8 at 11:59 p.m. ET, for trips taking place between November 28 and January 4. It’s limited to one use per guest, first-timers only, and capped at the first 4,000 redemptions. Additional terms apply.

There are definitely some cool and fun cars on Turo. You can rent yourself anything from a triple-black Land Rover Defender to a C8 Corvette to an FSD-equipped Tesla . With Turo Delivered, the car can also meet you at an airport, train station, hotel, or rental home, with no line or counter involved.

The peer-to-peer setup also means there’s a little more legwork—you’ve got to coordinate with someone from the internet, rather than just rolling up to a corporate desk. Pros and cons, right? But if you’re into cars or peer-to-peer programming in general, it’s a neat solution I’ve used a time or two myself.

Turo also sells digital gift cards for people who like to travel or are into cars on your holiday gift shopping list. Pick a design and an amount, then send it immediately or schedule it for later. Recipients redeem them on the app or Turo.com, and the credit never expires. Gift cards can only be bought and redeemed in the US.

items.title: Toyota Explains How It’s Trying to Fix Its Big Tundra Problem
items.summary:
Toyota, the world’s largest automaker, knows it has a problem: its Tundra truck engine is threatening its rock-solid reputation for reliability .

Now, the updated 2027 Toyota Tundra is arriving at dealerships and aims to address many issues with the current truck including but not limited to safety concerns with towing, infotainment limitations, ride quality issues, and more. Of course, Toyota’s angling for its change in machining processes for engine production to also hopefully fix its reliability issues. On the latest episode of The Drivecast , Toyota Tundra and Sequoia Assistant Chief Engineer Rob Crawford sat down exclusively with The Drive   to sort through the changes.

The Tundra ended up at the center of Toyota’s engine failure crisis . If you read The Drive or listen to this podcast, you know what I’m talking about. But for those who don’t, Toyota took a big swing when it introduced a 3.4 liter twin turbo V6 known as the V35A FTS in the current generation Tundra pickup and Sequoia SUV in 2022. It replaced the hardy 5.7 liter V8 used by those models for over a decade.

And at the time, a lot of people wondered if swapping a simple proven engine for a new high stress one would lead to problems. Sure enough, it did. The new V6 started destroying itself at notably high rates. As we’ve reported at length, including on this podcast back in June, the issue surrounds tiny bits of metal debris called swarf that get left behind in the engine block during manufacturing. Those shavings then adhere to the main bearing and cause knocking, rough idle, or total engine failure.…
items.t: Toyota Engineer Explains How It’s Fixing the Tundra

items.title: Here’s Why GM Never Built a Manual C8 Corvette—and Why Its Own Transmission Supplier Did
items.summary:
When Tremec told the world last year that it had developed a manual gearbox for the automatic-only C8 Chevrolet Corvette, the announcement created quite a stir. That buzz wasn’t limited to enthusiast chatter on social media; even Corvette Executive Chief Engineer Tony Roma commented on the existence (or lack thereof, at the time) of Tremec’s gearbox . Things got a bit tense, perhaps, and some were left with the impression that Tremec was dunking on GM for lacking the imagination necessary to make a manual C8 happen.

The real story, of course, is quite different. I touched on this in my brief write-up of the Peitz Performance swap , but here’s the longer version: GM’s decision had nothing to do with its engineering capabilities and everything to do with budgets. Roma has made no bones about it: a key component of the Corvette formula is affordability, and simply offering a second gearbox meant doubling the budget for an already whole-cloth transmission redesign.

“Transmissions are super expensive,” Roma told us on The Drivecast podcast ( the full transcript is published here on the site ). “When we had C5, C6, and C7, we could use basically the same manual transmission architecture that had been around and slowly developed over like 30 years, and it was mostly paid for, and we were doing slight upgrades on it, and it cost reasonable amounts of money to keep it in production.”

Byron Hurd, Andrew P. Collins 

What happened? Like everything else in the C8 (save the V8 itself, really), its fundamental design had to be thrown out the window due to the car’s mid-engine layout.…
items.t: Here’s Why GM Never Built a Manual C8 Corvette—and Why Its Own Transmission Supplier Did

items.title: New York’s Automotive Subscription Ban: Great Idea With One Big Loophole
items.summary:
In what appears to be a big win for consumers, New York just passed a law that bans automakers from charging subscription fees for options you already paid for. Sound too good to be true? Well, it kind of is, because there’s a gaping loophole that will pretty much guarantee that most subscription features will stick around for the foreseeable future: The new law doesn’t apply to anything that costs the manufacturer money to maintain. 

The good news is that this law will ban foolishness like BMW’s now-infamous subscription seat-warmers , which the company backtracked on pretty much immediately after widespread internet backlash . The bad news is that the entire “features as a service” fad will be left largely intact, because virtually all subscription services offered in modern cars require that they phone home to some sort of server in order to function. That includes features like connected navigation, emergency roadside assistance, and in-car hotspot plans. Here’s the actual language (emphasis added by the author):

S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost . As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

Basically, if it involves the automaker’s app, network services, or any other kind of service with an ongoing…
items.t: New York’s Automotive Subscription Ban: Great Idea With One Big Loophole

items.title: Genesis Exec: Magma SUVs, Performance Hybrids Coming, but Brand Won’t Just Be a ‘Badging Exercise’
items.summary:
A few years back, Genesis showed us its first concept for a new “ Magma ” sub-brand. With blazing red-orange colors, its prototypes suggested a performance bent, but we were told that the sub-brand would stand for more than just going faster. When pressed, Genesis execs said to focus on the “more” part rather than the object that followed it. Magma would simply mean more —more performance, more luxury, more personalization. And of course, more profitable for Genesis.

Since then, we’ve seen Genesis suggest that its new sub-brand might go racing . Well, now you’re speaking our language. That suggestion was accompanied by a mid-engine supercar concept that looked suspiciously similar to an existing American offering . So that’s what “more” might look like on the track. What will it look like in showrooms? To find out, we met with Ash Corson, who runs product planning for Genesis. Turns out, Corson has his hands full developing the Genesis sub-brand. 

“It can’t just be a, you know, a badging exercise,” Corson told us. 

Part of the problem, at least in his eyes, is that some of the established German manufacturers—the manufacturers who invented the entire concept of a performance sub-brand—have lost the plot. 

“There’s been an over-indexing—a dilution of the brand, if you will,” he elaborated. “We want to make sure we avoid that. Our first ‘proof is in the pudding’ vehicle is the GV60 Magma.”

The 640-horsepower electric crossover may not be a traditional enthusiast’s idea of a performance car, but it has the attention of the industry, Corson said.

“We pulled it off thanks…
items.t: Genesis Exec: Magma SUVs, Performance Hybrids Coming, but Brand Won’t Just Be a ‘Badging Exercise’

items.title: This Japanese Driving School’s Nissan Skyline Sedan Is GT-R Cool Without the Badge (or Price)
items.summary:
Who doesn’t love a Nissan Skyline? There’s no questioning the GT-R’s legacy. At the same time, culture and history have contributed to a pervasive idea that the only R34 worth having is one with that famous red emblem , and that’s just not true. Take this sedan, for example. Not only does a four-door Skyline have a certain appeal, but this one helped many eager students learn how to drive, and wears a period-appropriate livery to prove it.

This 1998 Skyline GT was operated by a Yamasaki Driving School and is currently for sale on eBay with a Virginia title. (Thanks Barn Finds for the spot). Lest you think its provenance is a ruse, the seller claims to have all the original documentation certifying that this vehicle was indeed registered for instruction. Stickers in the cabin and on the windows remind occupants to buckle up, and in the passenger footwell—which, remember, is on the left side in this application—you’ll find a brake pedal. It even has a dash-mounted G-Force meter!

The story goes that this sedan was purchased at auction in Tokyo two years ago, with the intention of an RB26 swap. This particular model packs a 2.0-liter RB20DE “Neo” engine—the base, economy-grade version of Nissan’s stout inline-six, making just north of 150 horsepower new. The owner ultimately decided not to go the swap route, and instead preserved the Skyline as is.

butler_performance via eBay 

With 125,000 miles on the clock, this R34 had a very long service life; Yamasaki only stopped using it in 2020. Despite this, pretty much everything is said to be in excellent working order, from the…
items.t: This Japanese Driving School’s Nissan Skyline Sedan Is GT-R Cool Without the Badge (or Price)

items.title: Hyundai Is Serious About Taking On The Toyota Tacoma With Its New Midsize Truck
items.summary:
Hyundai is on track to introduce a new midsize truck by the end of the decade. Naturally, we’re curious how Hyundai expects to catch up to an established segment with buyers that are known to be brand loyal, to put it mildly. 

We asked Olabisi Boyle, Hyundai’s senior vice president of product planning and mobility strategy for North America, exactly who the target customer is. And Boyle was blunt about it: while Hyundai is certainly hoping some of its existing customers will embrace the new truck , the company lacks a baked-in customer base for body-on-frame pickups. 

Yep, that means poaching. 

“We would have to conquest, right, to some degree,” Boyle acknowledged. 

Hyundai’s target buyer is the kind of truck owner who expects to get 10 or 15 years out of their purchase. 

“These are practical buyers. These are people who just want dependability,” she said. “So one of the things that we have to do is prove credibility on things like frame and chassis. We have to capitalize on where the leaders are already weak and we kind of understand where that is,” she continued.

Hyundai reckons there are quite a few ways a new entry could make a splash in this contested market. And Hyundai is aware—keenly so—of just how many trucks the market leaders are selling. Toyota sells nearly a quarter-million Tacomas in the U.S. each year. That’s not quite full-size truck territory, but it’s nothing to sneeze at, either.

“And we have to definitely meet, but most likely exceed, where the leaders are in capability,” Boyle said. “We understand those areas really well.” 

Caleb Jacobs

items.title: GTA VI Handles Better Because Actual Racing Drivers Made It
items.summary:
With Grand Theft Auto VI somehow actually real, here, and in millions of people’s hands, we’ve finally had the chance to discover for ourselves whether the perceived car handling changes we thought we picked up in all those leaks months ago are legitimate. It’s pretty obvious that GTA VI’s physics have more going on under the hood than the prior game’s, but they’re not necessarily as sludgy as IV’s, either. They’re unique and vary greatly across a wide roster of cars, and we have pro drivers to thank for that.

Those who have kept a close eye on GTA VI’s development know that amid the billion-plus dollars Rockstar is said to have spent on making the game, it also put its vehicle physics team on very practical field assignments. Rockstar North, the Edinburgh-based studio responsible for directing the series, fielded a BMW 3 Series in the 24 Hours of Nürburgring four years ago . All three drivers—Ben Lyons, Markus Low, and Dale Lomas—work there; Lyons is actually the Technical Director in charge of physics. They won their class at the event.

They’re not the only automotive experts that have lent their insights to the game. Lewis Bentley, a former Gran Turismo World Series competitor, shared that he worked on GTA VI’s car physics in a video over the weekend. It’s likely they’re not the only talent involved.

The Porsche 718-aping Pfister Growler is extremely responsive and actually quite hesitant to kick the tail out. Everything behaves differently. The Drive 

It all helps explain why GTA VI feels the way it does. Here at The Drive , we started playing when the rest of you…
items.t: GTA VI Handles Better Because Actual Racing Drivers Made It

items.title: BYD Ti7 banned from the EU for copying the Land Rover Defender’s design
items.summary:
A Dutch court has barred BYD from selling or building its Ti7 SUV anywhere in the European Union after ruling that it infringes Jaguar Land Rover’s registered design for the Land Rover Defender. Breaking the injunction costs BYD €100,000 per day, up to €10 million.

It’s a sharp turnaround from 10 days ago, when the same court in The Hague handed BYD an early win in the Defender copycat fight . BYD’s Hong Kong shares fell as much as 4% on Monday before closing 1.9% lower.
